alt: Questionnaires use closed questions, which give quantitative data, or open questions, which give qualitative data. Interviews are structured, with the same questions in the same order, or unstructured, like a conversation. Cards give a strength and weakness of each, and a warning that social desirability bias threatens both.
caption: Closed and structured questions are easy to compare; open and unstructured ones give depth.

alt: A tally sheet with four categories for observing personal space in a library, filled in by two observers with illustrative tallies. Three steps check inter-observer reliability: observe the same people at the same time, record independently with the same categories, then compare tallies; high agreement means the observation is reliable.
caption: Two observers, same categories, recorded independently: agreement shows reliability.

alt: Three scatter diagrams with illustrative points. Positive: hours on social media rise with loneliness. Negative: more close friends goes with lower anxiety. No correlation: shoe size and conformity show no pattern. Below, a stressful job is shown as a third variable that could raise both social media use and loneliness, so correlation cannot show cause and effect.
caption: Correlation shows a relationship and its direction, never cause and effect.

alt: Quantitative data (numbers) is easy to analyse and tends to be more reliable but can lack validity about feelings; qualitative data (words) is detailed and often more valid but harder to analyse and less reliable. Primary data is collected for the study and fits the aim but takes time; secondary data, such as government statistics, is quick but may not match the aim.
caption: Numbers favour reliability, words favour validity; primary data fits the aim, secondary data saves time.

alt: A dot plot of the ten anxiety ratings on a 1 to 10 scale, with three dots at 6. The mean of 6.5 is marked with a dashed line, the mode and median are both 6, and a bracket shows the range from 3 to 10, which is 7. Cards give each calculation and its strength or weakness.
caption: Mean 6.5, median 6, mode 6, range 7: four summaries of the same ten scores.

alt: Twenty-four circles, eighteen shaded for bystanders who helped and six dashed for those who did not. The same result is written as the fraction 18/24 = 3/4, the percentage 75%, and the ratio of helpers to non-helpers 18:6 = 3:1. A note suggests estimating first: a bit less than 80%.
caption: 3/4, 75% and 3:1 all describe the same 18 helpers out of 24.

alt: Four small panels: a frequency table with score and frequency columns; a bar chart with gaps between bars for separate categories; a histogram whose bars touch for continuous data in intervals; and a scatter diagram with one point per participant for correlations. All values are illustrative.
caption: Gaps for categories, touching bars for continuous data, points for correlations.

alt: An illustrative symmetrical bell-shaped curve. A dashed line at the centre marks the mean, median and mode, which are all equal. Most scores cluster around the middle, with fewer at the extremes on either side.
caption: Symmetrical and bell-shaped: mean, median and mode all sit at the centre.
